utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you see, I don't even wait for the interpretation now. Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. My name is Andrew Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor with case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cayley, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, along with co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. I understand, Mr. Ackerman, you've got some issue to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, these come under the category of loose ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll go through them as briefly as I can. There were two matters that arose on the 10th of April. The first one had to do with a couple of tapes, Prosecution Exhibits 509 and Prosecution Exhibits 508. And you'll probably recall that the dates were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't be too optimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The dates were represented to you on those tapes as being 1992 and 1993. Then looking at the tape that was represented as 1992, it became clear that there was a poster on the wall that said "1994." It was also clear that Mr. Cayley only made that representation to the Court because that's what he was told by someone. We had a very long discussion about it, and I made a request: "All I'm asking Your Honours to do" - and this is -- I'm quoting from my request - "is ask Mr. Cayley to look into this matter and advise us how it came to be that that tape was represented as coming from 1992. And if further investigation is then required, that it be carried out and that care be taken regarding representations of that kind." I then said: "This, Your Honours, is the mischief of what I think is a loose and reckless way that we deal with evidence in this Tribunal." And I'll speak about that a little further in just a minute. Mr. Cayley then said: "I will look into this myself. I will have investigations done to certainly date these tapes properly and will also endeavour to find out where the date of 1992 came from in respect of the representation that I made." And then a little further on, Your Honour, Mr. Cayley said again: "I will. I will investigate. I will give Mr. Ackerman that information and then I will give it to the Court." And then Judge Agius: "Yes. And as soon as you have the information that Mr. Ackerman suggested we request from you, please let us have it."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Yes." And I'm wondering with regard to that particular one - and I've got others - if there has been a such follow-up and what that result was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also think that in either the subsequent sitting or the -- anyway, a subsequent sitting, in any case, Ms. Korner came forward and more or less gave a semi-explanation, promising even further information later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're probably right. I don't recall that. You're probably right, Your Honour. The next one, Your Honour, was on the same date. It happened -- and I think just as a matter of caution, we should go to private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of the two videotapes, what I can say is this: The reason that the representation was made as it was by me was in reliance on what a prior witness had stated as the date of the videotape. I've reread the transcripts, and that is the conclusion that I came to, that that is why I -- I suggested that date because that is how a previous witness apparently mistakenly had dated this particular tape. What I -- what I did discover subsequently is that the Bosnian government had actually given us the correct date, and that is where we failed, because in putting this tape originally into evidence the ERN -- the IF form registering the evidence had not been consulted. Why that wasn't done, I don't know. But the Bosnian government actually provided us with the correct date, and then subsequently we had a witness date that material in the courtroom and that was the incorrect date. So that is the outcome of that inquiry. As to the document that Witness BT11 was going to procure on our behalf, a document was acquired from him and the reason that it is not yet before the Court is because it's being translated. And as you know, there is a huge translation backlog. And because of the fuss that was made about that document, I didn't want to offer it to the courtroom until such time as we had a CLSS translation of the document that he was referring to. And as soon as I do have a translation, I will give a copy of it to Mr. Ackerman, and to the Defence team for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Presumably this is -- this is the kind of document that I would expect not to exceed one page. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour. But it goes in a queue. That's the problem. And to be honest with you, I knew I'd received it. Mr. Ackerman mentioning -- it's reminded that it's gone into the system and I will find out where it is in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now let's go into private session please. Or you can deal with the Rasula -- what arises from Rasula's diary and then we'll deal with the last part in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The -- the last point that Mr. Ackerman made is, I think, something that Ms. Korner and I need to discuss, because if that is a project that is going to be launched where we have to check every single copy against every original document, that is a huge undertaking. And if that is a challenge that is being made, then that is something that we may have to consider doing. But I would like to discuss that. At the moment, I simply don't know whether we have the resources to do that. And I don't actually believe it is a prevalent problem. That is my view. I think it is an occasional problem. And in the case of this size -- and I've done two of these cases before -- it does arise occasionally. But the great majority, the vast majority of the documents are, I believe, true copies of the document that we originally received in this office. I think it would be best if the Defence and the Prosecution identified those documents together where there is some question about that or a particular document having some mark on it about which there is a query, and then we can look at those documents. But to do a complete survey of every single document in this case is quite frankly a huge task to be looking at. So I put that out as a suggestion, as a way of solving the problem that Mr. Ackerman has identified. And if we can go into private session for the last point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Cayley that the vast majority of documents in this case are probably true and correct copies. And again, I think I've been misheard. All I was asking was that those documents which have unidentified writing on them that doesn't necessarily appear to have been part of the original should be checked against the originals because that's what happened in the -- in the Rasula thing. And I think there is -- there ought to be among Your Honours a concern that there be a pretty high degree of integrity in the documents that you're being asked to -- to use for the purpose of finding people guilty of the most serious crimes that they can possibly be charged of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can rest assured, Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Cayley, that if there is even the slightest doubt about the integrity of a document, we will just throw the document where it belongs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But could we at least agree a process, because -- I think we're actually of one mind. I mean, I agree with Mr. Ackerman. If a document has some kind of suspect mark on it, we should actually track that document to the end of our road to see what the original looks like. What I'm saying is at the moment I'm not sure what documents he's referring to. I know the Rasula's diary. But which documents? I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I frankly think from the documents that I have seen I've really come across very few documents with what seem to be handwritten additions or -- or cancellations or substitutions. I don't know. And I would imagine that a good number of these additions are not important. However, they may be of absolutely -- of paramount importance, as was the case in Rasula's diary. So I think we will have to take them as we go along and -- I don't think that the -- that I can raise any complaints against the Defence for having raised such objections unnecessarily or capriciously, because they have only come up with objections on one or two occasions. And in one of them, at least, they were proved right. So I think we -- we have to be very cautious. And I think it would be very stupid of -- of the Prosecution or of the Defence to embark into a mammoth task of going through all the documentation to check pre-emptively. I think you have to go as we go along. And if there is a question raised with regard to a particular document with super-added annotations or additions or whatever, then -- then we deal with that as we go along. I mean, I don't see any other sort of practical solution, Mr. Cayley. Because otherwise to ask you to go through all the documentation would be to -- to expect the impossible from you. You know, I mean, not with all the work that you already are encumbered with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So are we agreed, then, that what will happen is with all future documents, if it arises again, we will take the original document out of the vault and check it against the original document? For all past documents, Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Fauveau will identify those that they have a problem with and then we can go to the vaults for the document then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example -- for example, I have -- I remember seeing documents with a handwritten note saying just "Top Secret," or for example, with the word "Prisoners of war" cancelled or obliterated or a few other things. I don't know. If the matter is brought up, then I think it needs to be investigated. If it's not brought up, it -- it -- basically we take it that it is not that substantive or that important to really go into. But if it's worth going into, we'll go into. But the onus is always -- I need hardly repeat that. The onus is always on you. And the ultimate word of -- of the -- the last word of the Chamber is that we always reserve the right when we come to the end of the -- of the exercise that if we find ourselves having to rely on a document, the authenticity of which we honestly doubt, then we are not going to rely on it. It's as simple as that. It's not a question of coming back to the trial and then inviting you to go over and restart the evidence on -- on that particular document. I mean, at a certain point in time the curtains will fall and we will start doing our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is not the agreement that we will identify for the Prosecutor the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not. I mean, I don't expect you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If at the end of this case there are documents we believe have not been properly authenticated, we will make that argument and ask you to exclude them from evidence. And if the Prosecutor has not properly authenticated them, that's their problem, not ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, no. That's how I see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the second -- the second thing: We've seen another example today -- I mean, we've got three now. We talked to you -- we complained about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher -- one moment. Usher, please go to the room where the witness is and explain to him why he's being kept there and that we will soon be calling him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We complained about the Rasula diary, that it was not authentic, and it turned out we were right. We complained about the date on those two tapes, the date was wrong, it turned out we were right. Now we learned today that the Prosecutor had in their possession a document dating those tapes properly and permitted a witness to testify to a different date and didn't clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That could be an oversight. I mean -- I mean, I appeal to you to be reasonable here and concede that the Prosecution, like you, is not -- and like me is not infallible. So that may have been an oversight, and I am prepared to consider it, give them the benefit of the doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am too. I am too. But how many of these must we say is -- are a result of oversight and how many of them are a result of just not properly -- I mean, if they were required by Your Honours to lay a proper foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- in which they would have to establish the date of the tape, this wouldn't happen. And that's why it happens. They don't have to look for the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. Let's go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, you can bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to repeat the -- once more the solemn declaration, please, before you start your evidence again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And before Mr. Cayley continues with his examination-in-chief, may I kindly ask you to accept our apologies for keeping you waiting in that room for 35 minutes. The reason is that, as it happens sometimes, we had a procedural problem -- more than one procedural problem that we had to attend to, and that took us some time to resolve. So my apologies. And Mr. Cayley now will resume with his direct examination of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed. Examined by Mr. Cayley: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. Could you direct your mind to the meeting --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you direct your mind back to the meeting that we were discussing yesterday on the 28th of July of 1992 with Mr. Vrkes and other Serb leaders. And you had explained to the Court yesterday how you discussed with him the fake shelling of your village that had occurred on the night of the 26th and the 27th of July. What I'd like you to do now is tell the Court what other discussions you had with Mr. Vrkes concerning the Muslim population of Pobrijezje on that day.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after what I have already informed you about, we asked Mr. Vrkes to examine the possibility of going to have discussions with UNPROFOR in Topusko, or rather, the north sector, because there was announcement over the radio that had been broadcast during those days that part of the Muslim population from Bosanski Novi had managed without big difficulties and problems to get to Karlovac with the help of the UN. And that seemed like a very acceptable option in that period to us for the following reason: Because it would be guaranteed that families wouldn't be separated and that all those who wanted to leave with those convoys, who would certainly reach the destination, would reach Karlovac. We asked him to examine that possibility and if possible to make it possible for us to go to Topusko to Dvor Na Uni to talk to official representatives who at that time were staying in the sector west in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just show you a map --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which, Your Honours, I'm not going to exhibit. This map is actually already in evidence but it's under seal because the last witness who referred to it was a special witness that I can't refer to in open session. But I think you may recognise the map. And I don't want the put the map into evidence again, because it just simply increases the number of exhibits. But if you could place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if, Witness, you could just show Their Honours the location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the exhibit number at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll get Ms. Gustin to give you the exhibit number. But you do have this map already. If you can place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You look at the map on the ELMO over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could move it to the right -- I'm sorry, to the left. To the left. Actually, can you hand it back to me. Because I think we're looking at completely the wrong part. It's P773, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's P773.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you can see on that map, Witness, Banja Luka. Can you point out Dvor and Topusko, if you can. If you can recall where they are on that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if the Banja Luka map could be moved so that Banja Luka is right in the centre and then you have that part of the map enlarged --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know where --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You need to bring the camera out, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you need to move it slightly to the right. Perfect. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at the map on the projector, I think you'll be able to see it more easily. I'm sorry to put you in this position. I should have marked the map in advance, but -- can you just point to Topusko.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi and then to the right you go towards Dvor Na Uni and this is the way you go towards Topusko. It's somewhere here, just a minute. Bosanski Novi, Topusko. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see that Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's just into the Republic of Croatia. I just thought I'd show you the place we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been mentioned by another witness, that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, thank you for that. Can you describe to Their Honours what conditions were like at the end of July and beginning of August in Sanski Most for you as a Muslim living there.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the tension had increased. People were intimidated, and the life and existence of the Muslim population during that period was not certain. It was under a question mark. And for these reasons there was increased activity to voluntarily move out, in inverted commas, in order to save one's life and save the lives of one's family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after your meeting with Mr. Vrkes, did you in fact go to Dvor Uni to have this meeting with the UN?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I'd like to say a few introductory sentences to say how this trip to Topusko came about. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this conversation with Mr. Vrkes, I informed other citizens and I asked Vrkes at that time for him to make it possible for a meeting to be held at which more representatives of local communes who wanted the same would be present and would be able to present their positions and their requests and say why they wanted to go. I wanted this for several reasons, one of which I will mention. At that time there were various contradictory ideas about me in the town. According to some I was accused of cooperating with the Serbian authorities, and according to others I was trying to get people to move out of the town and not from Pobrijezje. And at that joint meeting I in a certain way wanted to prove that this was false and I wanted to hear the opinions of other representatives of local communes. Before going to Topusko, the president of the municipality, Mr. Rasula, made it possible for us to have a meeting at his office. On that day there were 28 representatives who were present. And they expressed their opinions, put forth their positions, with regard to this matter. It was clear to me that we were on the same wavelength and that we had the same objective, which was to save our lives, not to have our families separated, and to move on to territory which was more secure. At the end of that meeting, Mr. Vrkes told me that we should write something down on paper -- write down what the result of that meeting was and what I should say before the gentleman in Topusko, which is what I did. And a day before going to what at the time was still called Topusko -- and in fact that was going to be a departure for Dvor Na Uni, Vlado asked me to inform him, to tell him of the contents of the text that I intended to present with regard to the reasons of the non-Serbian -- or rather, Muslim population, with regard to the reasons that they had for wanting to leave. Your Honours, I want to emphasise in particular the circumstances under which I participated in that discussion. I entered Mr. Vrkes's office, which is on the square in Sanski Most. It's on the first floor. And there in the office I met someone who was well known to me, a well-known person, a parent of a school friend of mine; that was in fact, Brajic, a man who had lost two sons on the Croatian battlefield. And Vlado told me, "There's no problem. Please go ahead and read what you have brought with you." And I wanted to present the truth in good faith. I didn't write that text myself, but it was with the help of a -- a wider circle of people. And what happened? I wanted to emphasise that relations between the Muslims and the Serbs had been good up until that period in Sanski Most, and I wanted to point out how diligent the Muslim population were in all segments of life, beginning -- from agriculture, the catering industry, industry -- geologists, lawyers, and I wanted to point out that this coexistence was really at an enviable level. I also pointed out that -- I pointed out what I thought I should point out. I pointed out the 26 religious buildings, that is to say, mosques, up until that point in time in the municipality of Sanski Most had been destroyed. Similarly I pointed out that certain establishments and certain houses -- and I mentioned the shop of Fajdo Banovic in Gornji Kamengrad where Basara Seno [phoen] had food and drink -- had enjoyed food and drink. I also mentioned the last list which -- the last sentence which reflects the population of Sanski Most. And at that moment it wasn't important to us. But it did show that 47 per cent of the population was Muslim in Sanski Most. And finally, with regard to other experiences and conversations, I pointed out that the Serbian authorities in Sanski Most, especially at these meetings, who were -- I was following this report from Mr. Rasula. I said that they weren't in a possibility -- in a position to ensure security for property. They weren't in a position to provide education, to ensure the right to work, to pension schemes and to medical care. In such a situation, the Muslim population in Sanski Most -- the possibility of them surviving, living, was put under threat. After I had read out that text -- and this was ironical -- it was a David and Goliath situation. I was very small and he was very powerful. And I was there in the presence of a parent who was suffering. And the Muslim people are certainly not to blame for this person's death. Ranko, his son, was a school friend of mine, and I was under a strong impression of suffering and pain. And I was asked, "Besim, what do you think? You're not going to congress? Please. It doesn't make any sense. And when we're talking about religious buildings, that can't remain. That part can't remain in the text, cross it out." And talking about Sanski Most, it was always a Serbian town. That's what they said. So the gentleman corrected my text. I could do nothing else. I only had -- I could only listen to him and do what he said I should do and hope that perhaps some circumstances would be in our favour and then we would be able to attain our objective. That was the discussion we had before we left. That was the first Sunday in August, when we left for Topusko. Unfortunately we went to Dvor Na Uni and we were to go to Topusko later. The justification for not having a discussion in Topusko was that there was no official person there who would be able to receive us there -- meet us there and talk about this subject. So on that day we returned without having carried out our work. That was toward the end of August. And then they set another date. I heard that would be in ten days' time, ten days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that ten days later you went back to Topusko?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what date the second meeting was or the day when you went back to Topusko? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember it very well. It was the 19th of August, 1992. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just wait one moment. How do you know it was the 19th of August of 1992 that you had that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those days remain imprinted in memory. An additional reason is that I later met this gentleman and he offered me the United Nations charter and the statute of the international court, instead of the business I had come to attend to, and I wrote the date down that. Gentleman was Sergio, head of sector north. And that's a sad momento from that period that I have kept to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who accompanied you to Topusko on the 19th of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the trip to Topusko, in addition to myself as a representative of the Muslim people on behalf of Sanski Most, there was a gentleman called Eso. I need to say here that it is a person from the territory of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, the village of Arapusa. Eso and his fellow citizens - there were about 600 or 620 of them - who on the 1st of May, 1992 were expelled from those villages and were put up in Donji Kamengrad in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was Esad from Bosanski Krupa accompanying you to Topusko?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went because a part of the conversation with Mr. Rasula had to do with the fact that they don't belong to the municipality of Sanski Most, that they were a burden to the people there because the locals don't have enough food to survive on and that it would be logical to find a way for these 600 or 620 of them to find a way to move somewhere else. And so Eso went on behalf of those people who had been expelled from Arapusa and Karapinja [phoen] which belonged to the municipality of Bosanski Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can remember the names of the other people who accompanied you on that trip.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first car, in addition to me and Eso, there was Mr. Vrkes and Mr. Majkic, the head of the security station in Sanski Most, Majkic Dragan, a mechanical engineer who used to work in a factory in Sanski Most. In the second car -- I didn't know at first when we left, but there was a driver called Vlasto and Lieutenant Colonel Anicic. When we got there, when we got to Topusko, then I learnt that they were there too. I wish for a moment to describe this part of the trip. We went via Prijedor. We didn't turn right next to the Prijedor municipality and the police station, but we turned left and took the old road to Bosanski Novi. As we entered the main highway, the Prijedor to Bosanski Novi highway, there was a major checkpoint there. Why am I telling you about this? I'm telling you because I was dreadfully frightened. I saw people there who do not belong to the region of Sanski Most and Prijedor, people with long hair, long beards, decorated -- using as a decoration a big poster of Mr. Seselj, a citizen of Yugoslavia and an inhabitant of Belgrade. At that checkpoint Mr. Vlado asked me, "What do you think, Besim, if they stop us?" And I said, "What do you mean? Surely you're our leader and I'm safe with you." "God only knows whether either of us are safe," he said, and I was really scared. Then we as went on on the way to Topusko on the 19th of August, 1992, as we crossed the bridge linking the two banks of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia he said, "Soon there will be no border here. All this will be one. All this will be Serb lands." I just said that I had no influence over such matters and that they knew best, and we went on to Topusko then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present at the meeting in Topusko from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting a certain Sergio introduced himself, de Mello I think he was. I can't remember the name well. And there's another representative of the UN whose name I really don't remember. There was a young gentleman called Dragan from Zagreb. He acted as interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man Sergio, was his name Sergio de Mello?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to pronounce it properly. Was it de Mello, de Melli? I think you're right. That was his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other UN official who was present at this meeting whose name you do not know, was he a local man? Was he from the former Yugoslavia? Or was he from somewhere else in Europe as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly was not from the area of Yugoslavia. He was a person like Sergio from some other country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what happened at that meeting briefly.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As briefly as I possibly can. Mr. Sergio received us. An introduction was made by Mr. Vlado Vrkes who briefly elaborated on the question of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the interests of the Serbian people. And finally he said that the Serbian authorities in Sanski Most wanted to meet the wishes of the -- of the Muslim population by bringing them here because we wanted to communicate under the banner of the United Nations's reckoning that we would be safe there. The second to take the floor was a young gentleman. I'm glad to see such young, educated people. A man called Pasic, representing Bosanski Novi. As soon as he started speaking, I realised that he was radical in his views, and he recounted briefly -- I think he mentioned the figure of 4.000 Bosniaks or Muslims that had left Bosanski Novi, and he said at the end that he was pleased that that was so because it was highly questionable whether many of them would have survived if they hadn't left. The third to join in the discussion was a shortish man. I don't know his name. But after his comments, he didn't mention Prijedor specifically, I asked him to look into the situation regarding three Muslims being taken out of a car who were going for dialysis in the region of Carakova and he said that he was not aware of that situation and that he would indeed look into it. After that, it was my turn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you there for the moment. The man Pasic, who was he representing?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of Bosanski Novi municipality. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Serb or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb, in any event, sir. Only I and Eso were Muslims in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third man from Prijedor who you spoke about -- you spoke about Carakova and I think the event with your father-in-law. Did he say anything else about Muslims in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything in particular except the tensions and that the intentions of the Muslim people in Prijedor were similar to ours, that they too wanted to leave Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after this presentation has been made, it's your turn to speak. And what did you say at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said briefly what I -- what was left in the document after the editing made by Mr. Vrkes in Sanski Most. So I highlighted good-neighbourly relations that existed before these unfortunate events among all the peoples in Sanski Most, including the Serbs and the Muslims. I emphasised the hard-working nature of the people there and noted - and this was permitted to me - that the Serb authorities could not provide personal and property security, the right to work, healthcare, and all the other things that I mentioned. Also in -- I mildly disagreed with Mr. Vrkes and said that Sanski Most was not Serbian but that it was Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian, and if we were to go back into history - though it was not the time for history - I said that I thought the gentleman was wrong but I realised why he was saying what he was saying. Because in that period even the skies were Serbian, the mountains were Serbian, the rivers were Serbian. Everything was Serbian. As if life had begun with the appearance of the SDS in 1992, but that was not acceptable because it was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had made your statement, what happened next in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised -- and that was towards the end of this meeting -- when Mr. Sergio said and asked the Muslim representatives to stay behind with him for a moment alone with him. To tell you the truth, I said there was no need because I had said what I had intended to say, because I was afraid that if I were to say something that I hadn't already said that this would have repercussions for me. But Sergio insisted, so I stayed behind. In this conversation when the two UN representatives, Dragan the interpreter, and myself and Eso were present I said and warned Mr. Sergio with the words, "Sir, you've already said that you would not allow -- that the UN would not allow resettlement from these areas. I understand from the administrative point of view, but I am warning you that a convoy has already left via Skender Vakuf and the Vlasic plateau, and it's highly uncertain when you go on a convoy like that. You don't know whether they will reach their first destination Travnik." He said, "I'm sorry, I can't do anything about that now." And then he gave me this UN charter as consolation. I went on to mention that in Sanski Most there was a lot of disturbance. There was shooting at night, burglaries, looting. I didn't mention any number, but I said that a large number of religious buildings had been destroyed, everything that had been redacted from the document of Mr. Vlado I told him. I said that there were two major attacks on the Trnovo local commune and the Hrustovo local commune. The Hrustovo incident was indeed painful. A large number of civilians had been killed, women and children and babies, and I had taken with me an old map of Sanski Most but you could see the local communes on it and I wanted to show him where Hrustovo was situated. At that point he said, "I know." And he pointed his finger at his neck. This gentleman knew that there had been slaughtering in Hrustovo, in addition to the killing in the village and the bridge and that people had been thrown into the Sana River. This caused me even greater pain. So that was what I said. And then Eso briefly told him how they had been expelled from his homes to Sanski Most. And he pleaded with him, he begged him to help 600 or 620 of them who are not inhabitants of Sanski Most to leave. And then we returned to town alone. If Your Honours allow it, may I tell you an anecdote?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it's relevant to what we're speaking about, yes, witness, and briefly.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not relevant. But in those days, talking to Vlado, there was trading with the Muslims and I wanted to say that the five Serbs who came with us were arrested and us two Muslims were walking around Topusko freely. Colonel Anicic was a well-known name, and Vlado Vrkes too. But they were reproached for not having announced their arrival in the SAO Krajina, because after all that was another state. So that is what I wanted to tell you, it's anecdotal that they had been arrested and we were free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. de Mello stated to you that the UN would not assist in the movement of the population from Sanski Most, what did you say to him would happen to the Muslim population if they were not moved?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the people will find one way or another and that most probably -- most of them would get killed on the way. The only way out in those days was via Vlasic plateau, Sanski Most, Skender Vakuf, Travnik. That was the route. And that was indeed what happened, because the next convoys followed that route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk briefly about the convoys and -- as much as you can remember. What was the first convoy to leave Sanski Most? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I told Mr. Sergio that one convoy had already left at the beginning of August, that had already left via Vlasic. It was a convoy consisting mostly of Muslims from the left bank of the town, the district known as Mahala, a part of Muhici, Otoke and the town itself. Up to 1.000 or 1.500 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that convoy leave yourself?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had to take the main road towards Prijedor, where my house is, and I remember, because a good friend of mine left on that convoy, Maric Rasim with his family. But if you allow me, there were another two local convoys, if I can call them that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just -- let's just deal with this convoy first and then we'll talk about the local convoys in a moment. Can you describe to Their Honours what you saw in respect of that convoy, how many vehicles, how the people were arranged on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. To use the word "organisation" would be an exaggeration. People did as best they could. The Serb authorities allowed this convoy. I think there were more than eight buses. There were some private passenger cars, and I can't remember just now whether there were any trucks or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How full were the buses with people?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not full but over-crowded, sir. Packed full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you state -- I think you stated a moment ago that there were between 1.000 and 1500 people in this convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my personal assessment. I am trying to be as accurate as I can when talking about these things. Possibly there were more, but not less; that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your -- and I'm quite sure the Defence will put this to you -- I'm not going to put your statements to you. But in your statement of 1999 made to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that there were 3.500 people in this convoy. Now, as best as you can remember, what is the figure approximately for that convoy?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I would have to decide, I would decide for the figure of up to 2.000, because it's very hard. It's a crowd of people. They go by quickly. One is upset any way. And later on in town people were talking about it, and various figures were mentioned. So after all, the organiser of the convoy knew best, exactly how many people left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you didn't count these people, but we want to try and get it as accurate as we can. Who actually organised this convoy?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person with whom we discussed organised this convoy. The Serbian authorities in Sanski Most -- whether this was through the Crisis Staff, the main Crisis Staff, or through the president of the municipality or through the party. But there was a certain number of people who were present in all spheres. And I have already mentioned the number. I have already referred to these people. But I could also add that Mr. Banjac was involved in this movement of people and Mr. Susnica [phoen]. They participated later. In addition to Mikan Davidovic who was responsible for that and Vlado Vrkes and Mr. Rasula, and these close assistants of theirs. But these five to seven people were involved in it, and they were the people who made the decisions on the departure of convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people on the convoys, were they mostly men or a mixture of men and women? Were there any children? If you can give the Judges an approximate idea of that.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I most certainly can. There were all sorts of people there were children, women, old people, old women, men, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people leaving Sanski Most voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means, no. I've already given you the reason. They had to sign, in inverted commas, a voluntary certificate. And please understand, Your Honours, that in such a situation, in such an atmosphere the Muslims could not survive. It wasn't possible for them to survive. It wasn't good to have a Muslim name in Sanski Most. And as a result -- well, it's just -- what an irony to say that they moved out on a voluntary basis. People simply had to accept that, and they did accept it, and they signed a document saying that they were leaving voluntarily in order to save their lives because they could see no other solution. There was nothing to be done. At that point in time no one could help. No one could prevent this from happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago - and I interrupted you - two local convoys that preceded this convoy in 1992. Can you tell the Judges briefly about those two local convoys.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first local convoy consisted of citizens of Mahala. And after Mahala had been shelled, they had been forced out and expelled to Pobrijezje. On the first day of a religious festival, the Serbian army came out, Mico [phoen] and others, and the chief too, the chief of police, who was Majkic at the time and Tutic Adija and all these people, they rounded these people up. There were 1.080 of them in Pobrijezje. I had this figure. They were taken for Velika Kladusa, the 1.080 of them. The second convoy -- before the one that went through Vlasic, the second one consisted of citizens from Banjalucka Street, Stanicna Street, Aganovica Sokak, and part of the right bank of Sanski Most. The destination was Gracanica. I couldn't state this here with regard to that convoy for Gracanica. The -- I couldn't state how many people were on this convoy, this one that I have called a local convoy, but over a thousand for sure, women, children, and mostly elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in respect of both of those convoys, all of the people who were on them were Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslims. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to a convoy that happened in early September. I think the dates that you've referred to are the 2nd and 3rd of September of 1992. Can you tell the Judges about that convoy that left Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After returning from Topusko, I informed -- and Your Honours, this is something I have to say -- my movements took place on the main street, on the town square, the municipality building and the park. I informed people, I told people, that the United Nations would not be prepared to take the risk to move anyone out under the UN flag. I told them that this would not be possible. A meeting was very soon held in the meeting of the president of the executive board of Sanski Most, Mr. Mladen Lukic, who used to be my director in the communal services in Sanski Most. He met me at 8.00 in the morning. I asked him to do so, and I said, "Mladen, let's see what we can do, how we can deal with this matter." He said, "Well, these people who are responsible about that matter are here. Let's see about it." At that meeting, there were 14 representatives of the local communes. The composition was mostly the same. Mikan Davidovic, Vlado Vrkes, Milenko Stojinovic, Professor Banjac. I don't know whether Boro Savanovic came in for a moment or two, also a member of the Crisis Staff. And we discussed who in the local communes were interested -- how many people were interested. We obtained certain information. We realised that without 15 or 20 buses it wouldn't be possible to fulfil the Muslims' wishes, in inverted commas. So by the time all the necessary paperwork had been done, had been -- all the necessary documents had been found, by the time the tax had been paid, the electricity, the telephone, communal services, public utilities, that is, tax for agriculture, by the time we had received certificates from banks stating that there were no outstanding debts, by the time all this had been prepared and a form had been filled in and provided to the municipal services, having submitted all these documents you would receive a certificate stating that you had carried out everything that was necessary to do and that the person in question could leave Sanski Most. On the 2nd of September -- the 1st or 2nd of September and the 3rd -- but I'm more certain that it was on the 2nd of September -- these -- this action of ours was carried out, the organisation of the convoy, Skender Vakuf, the Vecici plateau, Travnik. That night was a very long night. In the morning I was in the local commune in Pobrijezje and 15 buses left directly in the direction of the north, towards Bosanski Krupa -- or rather, the local communes in Sanski Most, Donji and Gornji Kamengrad which covered Fajtovci, Husimovci, Demisovci, where the population from those places were. It -- in addition to -- next to the destroyed mosque there was a trailer that had been parked there. It was a long lorry. It was covered with a tarpaulin. And in that confusion, no one had any lists so we had to look to see who had lists -- I'd like to point out that the civilian police and the military police were there. They were escorting that convoy. Someone said, "I have a list from yesterday." And I said, "Okay. Well, just read it out. It doesn't matter what it is." That was the most difficult thing to do then. I simply -- we simply had to finish what we had started. I read out 120 names, the names of people who entered that trailer with a tarpaulin. There were women, children, old people, men. Quite a few people remained outside. That's the truth. Some of them I can't remember their names now. They said, "Well, what is this? There's not enough lorries. There are more people who want to leave." In half an hour or 45 minutes' time another two lorries came from the mine in Kamengrad, the coal mine. These were lorries with a trailer without a cover. They were -- they were for coal transport. But they were acceptable and people accepted them. No one called anyone out. People got on, if they were able to do so. They just got on the lorry. And that convoy left. So a convoy consisting of 15 buses. There were lorries in Gornji Kamengrad too, seven or eight. And there were these two trailers. And that was a very big convoy, one of the biggest convoys. We thought that there were about three and a half thousand -- three or three and a half thousand people who left in that convoy. As a negotiator my work finished on that day. If we're talking to negotiating with the Serbian authorities of the local communes. And I would like to emphasise that on the following day I found the driver, Sikman, who was one of the drivers in the lorries, someone I knew, and his wife worked with my wife in a shop, in a self-service shop in Sanski Most, and I asked him, "How was it?" He said, "Don't worry. Everything was fine. Everyone got through." Well, thank God. One's glad to hear that no one died from the list that I read out, because that would be something difficult to bear. And then after a certain time we received telephone calls from outside and were told about how things had developed, who got through, et cetera, and that's when I stopped working as a negotiator with the Serbian authorities with regard to the matter of moving out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions to clarify this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But we can do that after the break, Your Honour, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cayley. We'll have a break of 15 minutes, resuming at 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been asked to inform you -- and I -- as a result of that, I will inform you -- that there's apparently some kind of a problem with transportation. And the accused in this case are sometimes forced to sit in a little tiny room downstairs till as late as 7.30 before they're transported back to the Detention Centre, and I've been asked to bring that to your attention and ask that maybe perhaps you could look into it and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will certainly look into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why there's such a delay in transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First thing tomorrow morning, please, Madam Registrar. I'll look into it first thing tomorrow morning, because I don't think I'm in a position to do anything today in any case. But I will certainly look into it. Yes, Mr. Cayley, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to ask you a number of questions of clarification about the convoy that left Sanski Most at the beginning of September of 1992. To the best of your recollection, who escorted that convoy out of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy was escorted by members of the civilian and military police. So both police forces were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see civilian and military police with your own eyes at the scene of the departure?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the numbers involved in this convoy -- and again, I know that you did not count all of these people onto the transport -- in your statement to the Bosnian authorities of the 13th of February, you give a figure of 220 only, which I think is a mistake when one looks at the statement. And then in the statement of the 15th of February to the Bosnian authorities you give a figure that equates to 1.720 people. And then in the statement you made to the Office of the Prosecutor you said 3.500 people. Now, bearing in mind the number of vehicles that you identified as being involved in this convoy, if you had to give an approximate figure for the number of people on the convoy what would you say?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number of 220 refers to citizens of the Pobrijezje local commune who were in that convoy. And the total figure which I mentioned was two and a half to three, three and a half thousand. The number 780, I'm not familiar with this number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You say in one of your statements -- you say 220 people plus 1500 people from other villages, 1.500 people from other villages. That's in your Bosnian statement of the 15th of February. And then in your statement to the OTP of 1999 you say 3.500 people in that convoy. I think you may well have said approximately. I don't have it in front of me. Again, I know you didn't count these people onto the transport, but I think this is probably a matter that you'll be questioned about in cross-examination so I want to make it clear now. If you had to give an estimate here today, what would you say to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall try to be as realistic as possible. 220 citizens from the local commune of Pobrijezje left. That's a fact. 15 buses which were packed left. Seven to eight lorries left. And the two subsequent lorries with trailers which came to the local commune of Pobrijezje. But my statement may be closer to the truth, the statement which says that the total figure was about two and a half thousand. So that's the 220, let's say, and in these -- who were in these vehicles, and there were certain private vehicles too. For example, Badnjevic who left with that convoy stepped on a mine when he got out near Travnik and he -- he was wounded. So I can't mention the number of private cars which joined the convoy on a private basis. So Your Honours, it would be realistic to say that there were two and a half thousand -- about two and a half thousand people. That would be a realistic figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again I ask you the question that I asked you last time: Were these people leaving Sanski Most voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims from Sanski Most were not leaving on a voluntary basis. That -- there's no doubt about that. They didn't do that. I have to point this out. I don't want to be misunderstood. And I'm doing this in good faith. There was no room for Muslims in Sanski Most in that period. Please try to understand this. For example, in Krna [phoen] and Ulica my head and his head -- the price was the same on the market. No one would be to blame for him and to one to be blame for me. If you put yourself into such a position, would you deliberately lie? Would you say I'm going voluntarily? But I'm leaving in order to save my family, to save my children. So it really wasn't voluntary. People were forced to move out. Nothing was voluntary about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move ahead in time to the 24th of September of 1992. You're still living in Sanski Most. Rasula came to your house and asked you to go to a meeting in Banja Luka with him. Can you tell the Judges very briefly about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my duty as a negotiator came to an end when this convoy that we have mentioned left, when it left at the beginning of September. On the 24th of September, in the afternoon, in the street where my street is, Mr. Rasula turned up there. When I saw him, I was glad to see him to an extent and I was also slightly afraid. He was the president of the municipality and he was there on his own, almost 50 metres up to my home I met him, I said, "Good day, president." He said, "Good day Besim." "What brings you here?" I said. And he said, "Well, it's nothing very serious. But you know what it's about." I said, "Well, tell me. Do you want to sit down?" I asked him. He said, "No. Let's talk standing up." He said, "Vance and Owen will be coming to Banja Luka tomorrow. The president -- and he was referring to Karadzic -- wants representatives of the Muslim people to be present so that they can say why they want to move out." And my answer was, "Mr. President, well, isn't there anyone else, someone who is more educated than I am? Because these are high-ranking UN officials, and this is the president of the republic we are talking about after all." "No," he said. "Don't worry about it. All you have to say is what you already said in Topusko. You have to express the positions that you put forward before the Muslims." And I was incredulous again and said, "Am I the person who is to go?" And he said, "Yes. It wouldn't be good if no one went." So if that's the case, I said,"All right I'll go. Who's going to go with me?" He said, "I'll go with you." I said, "Fine." And that afternoon we agreed that on the 25th of September, in the morning, I should go out at 7.00 in the morning, go out into the main road and wait for Mr. Rasula and those who were going to accompany him. At the time I didn't know who those people would be. After a certain period of time, after he had left, I got on my bike and went up to the entrance into the city, went to see friends, people, in order to tell them that tomorrow it was necessary to go. And what should we say? I realised that every word was important. And the fact that Mr. Rasula told me that I should say what I had been saying up until that point -- well, I told them about this. So I consulted a few intellectuals who had remained in Sana, who hadn't left. We agreed -- and I agreed to go. At 7.00 in the morning Mr. President arrived on time. A car from the Sanski Most municipality was there driven by the municipality secretary, Mr. Djukic. And at the back behind Rasula a Croat, Mile Mlinar was sitting. I knew him from before because he worked in the brick factory in Sanski Most. So we sat -- we got in the car. And about 10.00, half past 9.00, if not a little earlier, we got into Banja Luka. And security on the streets was quite obvious there, especially as we were approaching the municipality building in Banja Luka. It was obvious that security had been stepped up and that movement was restricted. People were directed in certain directions. The president asked us to wait for a little while. He was probably searching for a way for us to get in, to go up there. And after a certain period of time he came and he said, "Let's go." We entered the building. I think we went up to the floor. And next to Mr. Radic's office, to the left, there is a hall for journalists. He said, "Wait here. You can smoke. Don't go anywhere. Vance and Owen haven't arrived yet. We'll tell you. We'll keep you informed." And that's what happened. We spent some time there. I don't know exactly when Vance and Owen appeared with a lot of people who were accompanying them. And the Banja Luka authorities were with them too, representatives of the Banja Luka authorities. They then appeared. But before that I approached a well-known person because we used to be in a football club, Podgrmec Sanski Most, Mr. Simo Drljaca. That was his name. I said, "Hello. What are you doing here?" He said, "I came here with the president. Why? Well, I wanted to talk to him. I heard that Vance and Owen were coming today." I asked Simo to check the situation for those people, the situation that the people who had been taken off the convoy were in. He promised and he said that he knew nothing about them. I am going to return to the subject I am discussing. And maybe Mr. Brdjanin knows this better than I do, because he was in that office. But about 8 or 10 metres from us the entire team went into the office of Chief Radic. We remained where we were. There was tight security. We kept at a distance. No one approached us. They stayed there for a while. At about 12.30, 12.40 from Mr. Radic's office our man, so to speak, Rasula came out and the president, whom I had recognised immediately because I had seen him on television earlier on and on Serbian Television earlier on. I knew that that was Mr. Karadzic and they headed in our direction. To be quite frank, we were sweating a bit, he greeted us in a quiet friendly manner and said, "Well, how are things?" And I was the first address him. We remained standing when we spoke to each other. We didn't enter the hall and we didn't sit down. It was -- a conversation that took place in the hall for journalists. And Rasula said, "Well, what's happening? Let's hear about it." And I took advantage of that occasion to tell the president. I told him, "Well, this is what I have to tell you and do what you like." The Serbian authorities in Sanski Most were not able to guarantee security for our property and for other things, which I have already mentioned. They weren't able to guarantee the right to education, to medical care, to pension schemes, et cetera, and that is the main reason for which the Muslims in Sanski Most just don't see a future for themselves. And being a professional man, a very experienced man, a psychologist -- and I am telling you this quite frankly because he left a strong impression on me. It is obvious that he is a professional man. He said, "Look, don't leave your homes." And this is something that I remember very well. He said, "Just don't leave something that -- place where you've been living for ages." He said, "The Serbian police are in Sanski Most. Be good neighbours, good hosts. Help the Serbian authorities. Help them establish themselves. You Muslims will work and we Serbs will wage war." So this is advice he gave me. And I said, "Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you for being so frank. But after these words of yours, I don't see how the situation for the Muslims in Sanski Most can improve." He turned to Rasula and said, "Well, see how these people can be helped later on, how can they find work. Let them work and we will wage war." He said, "Boys, this isn't going to take very long. This won't last very long. Calm down. When this becomes a Serbian state, those who want to remain will be able to remain and work and those who don't wish to remain, they will be allowed to leave Sanski Most if they so choose." And our dialogue finished and a Muslim joined in, a representative from Petrovac. I can't remember his name. Whereas Mr. Mile, who was with me, was not able to get a word in because that conversation didn't last for more than 15 minutes at the most. Mr. President -- the president Karadzic apologised but said that he really had to leave. Rasula stayed on with us for a while. He said, "Wait here for a while and then we'll see when we'll leave -- when we'll head back." And we didn't stay on much longer. On return -- when returning to Sanski Most in the car I asked Mr. Rasula -- I said, "Please go to the local radio in Sanski Most. Make an announcement and let the Serbs hear what the president said. Tell them what the president said, that the Muslims should work that, they should have -- that their property should be secure, et cetera." And I said, "Mr. President, we're like Apollo 11, is this dusk for us? We get up in the morning and wonder whether we're going to take off or not. And whoever wakes up in the morning says 'thank God, I'm alive today too'." And I had the moral right to tell him this because when Himza Hadzic won of the first elections, the late Himza Hadzic for the president of the municipality of Sanski Most. I approached him and I said, "Mr. President, congratulations. And I hope you'll be my president too. And he said of course, Besim. So I had the courage to be open towards him. Unfortunately that news was never broadcast over Sanski Most radio because no one tried to transmit the words of Mr. Karadzic. Even if they may not have been true at that moment they were encouraging, at least a little bit. But unfortunately it finished on the 25th -- my context on the 25th finished -- my context finished and then it was -- all we could do was try and save -- everyone was only able to try and save themselves as best they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that meeting with Karadzic, how did conditions become in Sanski Most for the Muslim population? Did they get better? Did they get worse?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the situation was somewhat better. There weren't that many explosions any longer. But after that there was work obligation for Muslims was introduced. The first group of people were sent to clean the rubble of destroyed buildings, private homes as well as religious buildings. And a certain number of us were sent to cut wood in the nearby local commune of Stari Majdan, some 10 or 11 kilometres from Sanski Most. This wood was intended for Serb combatants because they had no time. They were on the front, as we were told. So we did these jobs at that time, started doing this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The rubble -- you said rubble of destroyed buildings was cleared away by Muslims. Were you involved in that work personally?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The local religious building, the mosque in Pobrijezje, other people that I knew did the same kind of work in Sanski Most; others in other places, according to the local communes in which they lived. I personally also went to the woods in Majdan. And I wish to tell you the following, Your Honours, what I had to do at the time. I could write Cyrillic very well and I still do. I wrote such a nice letter in Cyrillic to a soldier who led us down there because I saw him mistreating some people behind a tree. And when I went home I said I will probably have some work duty in my public utility company where I worked, and I said the next day I would not come; I would go to my company. And he threatened to send the police to fetch me. He was a man I was afraid of. His name was Milosevic. He was not quite all there. I'll remember his first name in a minute. I'm telling you this because in front of three Muslims he took a blue envelope with the words "Mr. Ljubo Milosevic, Stari Majdan." I was explaining the situation for him so as to avoid any repercussions. He found this strange and ridiculous. What I'm trying to say that any hasty move by any one us could have far reaching consequences, including the worst. This was my period experience with Majdan and the cutting of wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform work duty throughout the rest of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was work duty. In 1992 was of a local nature. I've just been telling you about it. But I do know from reliable sources, talking to these people on the market, representatives of other local communes, that a certain number of people also went to work for the families of Serb soldiers who were on the front, who had old parents left at home or who could not do any work. So I know that they -- that some people went to help them. So this was also a kind of work duty that some people did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of February, 1995, the last train that God sent us. For 200 German marks to Banja Luka, 62 people in the bus, and in spite of everything I have to say thank you to this man because I saved my family. Banja Luka, Jajce, and near Turbe there was an exchange, there was a bus that came, there were representatives of the BH army who took us over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've described conditions in Sanski Most. Why did you stay until 1995 as a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good question, sir. In December 1994 -- no, in 1994 the situation worsened in Pobrijezje too. First a body, a corpse, arrived of Ado and Zena Krupic from the front, killed during work duty. Then another corpse from the local commune of Pobrijezje. On the 7th of November everything climaxed in Pobrijezje. Your Honours, we learnt to interpret a shot and an explosion. That night there were no shots or explosions, but in the morning a married couple, a man and wife, Omic Suljo and his wife Fadila were mutilated. A man called Rizo counted 11 knife wounds on the woman and 13 on the man. The man who bathed their bodies counted these wounds. This was something quite obvious for everyone, that the eleventh hour was approaching. This was the 14th to the 15th of December. And a month previously - and I wish to stress this - one of the negotiators who was with me, the late Kamber Teufik, he experienced a tragedy. His house was blown up. He lost his life in that explosion. His wife Ismeta was very badly hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question was why did he stay in Sanski Most until December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the events he is relating actually also refer to 1994/1995, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think -- I think he's explaining why he left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I mean, he has the ability to sort of tell in narrative form. I mean, I'm not suggesting we're going to contribute these crimes to the two accused, but I think it's probably best if he explains why he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Islamcevic, try to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll give my concrete opinion. Thank you, I will heed your warning. Let me tell you. I wouldn't have covered 3.000 kilometres without telling you about these three cases. But to give you a specific answer why I stayed behind: After these convoys, I received a fax from Osnabruk that somebody was providing guarantees for me and my family to leave. Since -- until the end of 1992 we hadn't learned the truth about Nalic Ismet and his destiny -- in 1993 that was one reason. In 1993 there was another reason. You had to go to Gradiska to renew a visa. When I could go to Gradiska I had no money. When I had the money, I couldn't reach Bosanska Gradiska, though I had a man there, Nijaz Smailovic from Podgrmec, a friend of mine. I am still friends with him. He comes to Sanski Most. This misfortune or good fortune - I don't know which - I could never have both the money and the necessary documents at the same time. Your Honours, that would be my specific answer to the question put to me by the gentleman. And I wish to add one further point: A wonderful Serb called Prastalo, he was a man who followed my life ever since I was a boy and he said the following, "Besim, I thought you were an intelligent man." I said, "I hope I am." "You waited for this child seven years. And if for no other reason, leave for his benefit and come back in five years or ten years but save him." In those days I also learnt another painful truth, that my late brother Islamcevic Sadmir had been killed at the Kupres front as a fighter of the BH army. What did this mean for a Muslim in Sanski Most? It meant a sentence the same night. A brother who had left on one of the convoys. Therefore, every minute in Sanski Most -- spent in Sanski Most after that event was a question of life or death. And thank God the opportunity arose for me to leave this route via Banja Luka. Again, I had problems in leaving because the head of the Secretariat for National Defence, Boro Tadic, a comrade of mine from the party, wouldn't let me. He came four months earlier from Grabez after I returned from work duty where I was beaten up and left without teeth. He said, "You can't leave." And I said, "But can't you see what was going on?" However, thanks to a set of various circumstances and some good individuals, I managed to put my name on a list. On the 9th of February there were 16 or 18 of us who left via Banja Luka. Additional people joined us in Prijedor and Banja Luka. And 62 of us arrived in Travnik. So much about this journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I've finished my examination-in-chief, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Who is going first? Yes. Now, Mr. Islamcevic, as I tried to explain to you yesterday you're now going to be cross-examined. We'll take it one at a time. And the first cross-examination is forthcoming from the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin. And lead counsel Mr. Ackerman will be cross-examining you. May I suggest to you, Mr. Islamcevic, please, to try and answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. If you try to give us more than answering the question, you will never get out of here. You will end up here day after day after day after day. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the -- some representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on 29 and 30 of July 1999. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It might be fair to you if you had a copy of that statement in front of you in case you want to refer to some part of it that I'm referring to, although I'm not going to spend very much time on it. I'll -- just to be fair to you in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who is taking care of that? Thank you, Ms. Gustin. Do you have it in the B/C/S, in the Serbo-Croat language or in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've just received it in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On pages 4 and 5 of the English version you're talking about your actual meeting up I guess in Topusko with the UNPROFOR representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Ackerman if one of your colleagues could direct the witness to the corresponding page in the Serbo-Croat version. Unfortunately I don't -- I don't have a copy myself, so I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the same pages in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
