utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So you should look at page 5, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a paragraph, sir, in your statement where you're talking about what it was you said to the UNPROFOR representative at that time. And it begins with: "The guarantees they were seeking," they, being the Muslim population of Sanski Most. Have you found that paragraph yet?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a copy in B/C/S for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it. It says "Garancije" here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There are about two paragraphs there that I want to just ask you about. You were talking about you wanted guarantees regarding a right to personal safety, property safety, right to work, right to education, right to medical care, and for those who wanted to leave the area they wanted safe passage. That was the essence of the presentation you made at that time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Rasula, who was also there, responded, did he not, that he was not opposing Muslims leaving in the area but could not guarantee safe passage and said, according to you, "There are our fools that we cannot control." He said, "There are people who have lost family members in Croatia. He implied that they would want revenge for some of the local Serb soldiers who were killed or wounded in combat." Correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Rasula, the president, said that to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The next part of your statement I want to talk about, again very briefly -- and we're going to come back to both of these in a minute -- and that's the meeting where you spoke with Karadzic on 25 September 1992 in Banja Luka. And you've already talked about that. He asked you why Muslims wanted to leave Sanski Most, and you told him that the Serbs in Sanski Most could not guarantee the safety of non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just that. That is correct, but not just that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. There's more. But that's one -- among the things that you told him, that was one of them; right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, if you look at -- it's on page 8 of the English statement. It starts with the language: "We continued to stand in the corridor." That's how the paragraph starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph on page 8, [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the statement that you made to the OTP says is "Karadzic asked me what was the reason for Muslims to leave Sanski Most. I said that the Serbs in Sanski Most could not guarantee the safety of non-Serbs. I also said there were basic requests like the right to personal safety and property safety." Right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that there were no guarantees for personal and property safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rasula was present when you told Karadzic these things, when you responded to his request; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told the people from the Office of the Prosecutor in this statement: "Karadzic told Rasula to do something about that." Right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your understanding of what -- basically what Karadzic was saying to Rasula was fix this problem. Do something about this, fix it. Right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why you wanted Rasula to go on the radio and tell the people of Sanski Most what Karadzic had ordered and what Karadzic had said.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before you gave this statement to the Prosecutor, on 15 February 1995 you gave a statement to a person named Zijad Ibric, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was this statement taken from you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taken after I arrived in Travnik in the centre of public security services, Travnik, in Banja Luka. That's how it was called, this institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Who is Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the man for the first time when I arrived there. I don't know what his duties were at the time. But anyway, he took the statement from me. I didn't know what his position was or his duties. But I assumed that he was from the state security service or somebody in charge of that institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he find you, or did you find him?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After receiving all the people who had arrived in that convoy, we were registered and I was invited to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not by him but by the service of the secretariat, of the Banja Luka centre secretariat, Travnik municipality. And the person represented that service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the number one -- I'm sorry, the first man I saw as I got off the bus at the exchange close to Turbe, the first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you though is: Do you know the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no. But he introduced himself when taking the statement and he gave his name, but it didn't mean anything to me at that time. When I got off the bus I didn't know the name of the man. The next day, when I was invited to make the statement and when I arrived at the office the man introduced himself and said what he was, who he was, and what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're speaking of Zijad Ibric at this point; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had understood you to tell us that someone else had asked you if you wanted to make a statement and had referred you to Mr. Ibric. And my question was: Who was that someone else, if there was someone else? Do you know that person's name?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to remember just now. I don't really remember who that person was who said "Come to this security services centre. You need to give a statement because you've just arrived from Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you last speak to Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 15 days ago or so, but exclusively about my coming here and in connection with my trip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he give you any kind of information regarding the testimony you should be prepared to give here?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you any kind of advice about how you should testify here?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you about the testimony of other people who had testified here?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than three to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you willing to say where you met with him?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know why not. Where did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How is it called? The entrance to the building where Mr. Zijad has an office, where he works in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he call you to meet him there, or how did it happen that you met him there?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed first by the relevant service of the Tribunal, because I was supposed to appear on the 3rd. Because I had to enrol my son at school in Sarajevo I asked this to be delayed, so that the next scheduled date was to be the 17th and I was ready to leave then, but then I was informed - and those are these three or five minutes - when he said, "Besim, you will probably receive instructions for another date." And then I was informed that that date would be the 21st, when I should be ready to come here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Informed by Mr. Ibric or by the service of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what was the purpose of your five-minute talk with Mr. Ibric? What did he actually tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know where Mr. Ackerman is trying to take this line of cross-examination. The witness has already answered what it was about. It's about a change of dates. Mr. Ackerman is looking for phantoms all over the place that don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's rephrase the question. You have already stated what more or less was exchanged in words between you and Mr. Ibric. Was anything else stated during that discussion, either by you or by Mr. Ibric in relation to your giving testimony here, or in relation to other people having given testimony here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can responsibly claim that there was no conversation. We didn't talk about me coming here and the testimony I was going to give, and very few people know when I was to leave and that I'm here. And with regard to anything -- with regard to this trip and the arrival here, there was no conversation. Nothing was discussed about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations prior to coming here with any other persons who have testified here within the last six months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That presupposes that he knows who they are. I mean, let's see -- Try to answer that question as far as you can. And if you're not happy, I will authorise you to mention names except names of protected witnesses, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's problem. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. Let me direct it and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll -- I'd be glad to answer that question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please understand do not say any names. The question is: Have you talked to anyone who has testified here previously? Please answer it just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when you spoke to Mr. Ibric back in February of 1995, the statement that you signed, that he asked you to sign, contained a great deal of information that was supplied by Mr. Ibric himself and not by you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense? When you say the number of pieces of information, what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me have you have a copy of the statement before I ask you any more questions about it. Just confirm for the record that you have in front of you the statement that you gave to Mr. Zijad Ibric on 15 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that statement in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you just look at the first sentence. The first sentence reads: "On 21 May 1992 I was working as a foreman at the market in Sanski Most." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it's 25th of May, not 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't come as a huge surprise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's exactly right; that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point I'm trying to make with regard to that sentence, sir, is this: One would get the impression that Mr. Ibric simply was writing down the things you had told him. And the first thing you told him was that on 25 May 1992 I was working as a foreman in the market in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated here is correct, that on that day I was working at the market in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the point I'm trying to make - and I'll try to make it as clear as I can - if one looks at this statement, it appears to be a statement made by you from information known to you, but in fact it contains information that was not known to you and supplied by Mr. Ibric himself. So it is significantly a statement of Mr. Ibric --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, could you tell me -- could you be more precise and tell me what you think is not my opinion here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you tell me if there are things in here that are not your statement that were supplied by Mr. Ibric. Am I correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, why doesn't Mr. Ackerman simply direct the witness to the part of the statement that he thinks was provided by Mr. Ibric and then we'll get there very quickly. For example, whether the personnel numbers -- the personal identity number that is the witness quotes in relation to various individual, whether he knew that or whether Mr. Ibric knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I prefer to get there my own way, Your Honour, rather than Mr. Cayley's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, if he identifies the parts that he says were supplied by Mr. Ibric, then the witness can actually answer the question and say, "Yes, that is something that Mr. Ibric put in or that is something that I put in."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is intelligent enough to know that the substance of the question is is this in reality your own statement or is this Mr. Ibric's statement. And he should answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But Mr. Ackerman is suggesting parts are not but he's not actually identifying the parts, then we play a guessing game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it's up to Mr. Ackerman to point those out, as you rightly point out. But first I think the witness needs to answer that fundamental question. Is this -- do you consider this to be your statement or is it in reality Mr. Ibric's statement which includes also parts -- bits and pieces of information that you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my statement, a statement that I gave to Mr. Ibric. But the personal identification numbers are not mine. How was I to know that, for that period, at that time. But everything else -- we can discuss everything else. I would have liked to have had this earlier on, to have been in a position to read it, and then I could have provided the Defence counsel with better answers. But the chronology of events, this is something that I put forward. But the personal identification numbers are not mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't the Prosecutor give you an opportunity to review this prior to your coming here to testify today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This particular statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to have a look at this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you given a copy of it to read?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that at various parts of the -- and we're going to go into them specifically in a minute. But I just want to generally suggest to you, isn't it the case that there were times during this statement when Mr. Ibric would tell you things that he knew to be true, that he believed to be true, and then tell you that you could then say that you know those things because he told you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to assist the Defence and everyone else here, I would like to say that this statement is mine, apart from the personal identification numbers. And any layman realises that at the time I didn't have this information on personal identification numbers. And this statement was given after four very difficult years, after many ups and downs. So please don't criticise me if there are certain shortcomings. But I really tried, both yesterday and today, to be as truthful as possible and to portray the events in Sanski Most in this period and with regard to the matters that are being discussed. So please don't involve Mr. Ibric in this statement of mine. Don't mix him up with this statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But may I ask you what form did the interview take? Was it in the form of a question and an answer, or was it a plain invitation to tell us -- to tell Mr. Ibric what you could remember or what he was interested in -- in knowing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibric asked me to try and concentrate and to narrate the chronology of events, to say what happened first, what happened afterwards. But as far as I can remember, there were no concrete questions, because I had only just left that territory. Perhaps there were a few questions, but I really couldn't say what sort of questions, what they regarded. But this is the chronology of events. This is the -- these are the events that I tried to describe as faithfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for example -- sorry, Mr. Ackerman. Just one moment, and I'll return him back to you. So for example, in page 2 when you mention dentist Mehmed Alagic -- you mentioned dentist Mehmed Alagic because you suddenly remembered the circumstances surrounding his death and not because he was mentioned to you by Mr. Ibric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, precisely, because at the time I was in Sanski Most I didn't see it but I heard a story from people who were in the immediate vicinity and saw when the late Mehmed fell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just stop. I'm asking you -- you mentioned Mehmed Alagic in your statement because you remembered the events and you -- and you wanted to mention his killing or because he was mentioned to you by name by Mr. Ibric during his interview? Who brought Mr. Alagic -- dentist Alagic in -- in the interview, you or Mr. Ibric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I introduced him. I remembered at a certain point in time as I was narrating the sequence of events. I suddenly remembered that. So this came from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with Mr. Ibric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop. Then you mentioned Zuhdija Bahtic, son of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How did the mentioning of Zuhidija Bahtic come into the interview? As a result of your initiative because you wanted to mention that person, or because Mr. Ibric asked you a question related to that particular person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to mention this person because I have family relations with -- from Gornja Mahala, I have friends about this. And this is the truth. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were you carrying with you this personal identity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1996 I exhumed that person and I saw him. 26 of them were buried in a mass grave, and among them were this gentleman that you have been asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talking about the 15th of February of 1995 when you are being interviewed by Mr. Ibric. Did Mr. Ibric ask you about Zuhdija Bahtic or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Mr. Ibric did not ask me about Zuhdija. That's something that I remembered, as you can see, as I was narrating the sequence of events. I spoke about the events that happened both before and later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you explain then in the same statement the moment you mention Zuhdija Bahtic you also give his personal identity number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I said, in this statement the personal identification numbers didn't come from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ibric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ibric had already the personal identity number of a person that he didn't know that you were going to mention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that. I can't say whether he had it or not. I personally don't know who put the personal identification numbers in. I didn't because I wasn't aware of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One last question before I return you to

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this interview started at what time and how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It lasted for perhaps -- it lasted for a while, but I don't know when it began. I've forgotten about this date. On the 9th I left. On the 10th I registered. I think I was there for over two and a half hours or three hours, in the building of the security services centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was it produced in writing in your presence on that same day? Was it typed out on that same day? Did you sign it on the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't written on the same day. I signed the written statement that was produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's back in your hands, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after your original conversation with Mr. Ibric did you actually sign a written statement?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than two or three days. I was called back two or three days later. And I have to tell the Defence and you, Your Honours, that I also noticed the personal identification numbers at that point and I said that I had no knowledge of them but that I would sign my statement insofar as this was the essence of what I had said, and that's what I've been trying to say today and what I tried to say yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The additional information with regard to many of these names that have supplied identification numbers also have information like Gojko Predojevic son of Djuro. Did you supply the, "Son of Djuro, son of Dzafer, son of Mirko, son of Petar"? Did you supply that information or did that also come from Mr. Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to tell the Defence that I am a child from the village. I was on good terms with all those people. They liked me and I never insulted anyone. And I know most of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibric has nothing to do with the names of the parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you supplied those.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an example, Predojevic Mladen [phoen] went to school with me. He's a brother. Probably two brothers have the same father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have to take it personally, Mr. Islamcevic. The question was a very simple one. When we see here Gojko Predojevic son of Djuro, are we to understand that it was you who told Mr. Ibric that he was son of Djuro or is it something that Mr. Ibric found himself from some document and then put it in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's what I knew at the time. That came from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That came from you. Okay. And this is the simple question. I mean, Hakija Islamcevic -- and it's son of Avdija. Was it you or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Islamcevic house is 15 metres away from mine, so this is something that I must be aware of. He's my cousin. And I know his family because we are related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you misunderstand that I'm not accusing you of not having this knowledge. I'm only trying to determine whether material in this statement came from you or came from Ibric. I'm not challenging whether or not you know things. I know you know things. So please understand that. Now, what I'd like you to look at is the -- basically this third line of the statement in English, and I think it's probably the third line in your language also, where you refer to the 6th Krajina Brigade and you call it "the infamous 6th Krajina Brigade." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say it right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the second sentence of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the security services centre in Banja Luka, in Travnik. That statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the statement that we have been discussing. The third line, "U to vrijeme zloglasna."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Third line after --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't found it yet. The third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's first page --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second sentence. First page, second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the middle of the page there is "Izjava." That's where your statement starts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day -- I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sentence reads: "At that time the infamous 6th Krajina Brigade." Do you see that? There may be a translation issue, sir. Why don't you just read the second sentence of your statement, begins with [B/C/S spoken], I think. No. It's the next one after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the next one, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, [B/C/S spoken]. Just read that sentence in your language.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of my friends said that something strange was being prepared, something strange was brewing in Sanski Most. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Do you see the very beginning of the statement that says: "On 25 May 1992," that we talked about earlier? "Dana 25/5/1992"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next sentence beginning with [B/C/S spoken]. The next sentence begins with [B/C/S spoken]. That's the sentence I want you to read.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At that time the infamous 6th Krajina Brigade or the so-called army of Republika Srpska was on the Jasenovac battlefield. It was already clear --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough. The word "infamous" was not a word that you used but a word supplied by Mr. Ibric, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you can claim that with certainty. I don't know why you are certain of this. You forget that I got out of hell, that I left hell, that I lost my brother. I lost my relatives. I lost 25 people. So is it strange if I should use the word "infamous"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your answer is no. Stop there. I mean, we don't -- and I think we need to stop too and we will resume in 15 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to -- we were talking about your 15 February 1995 statement to Mr. Zijad Ibric. Could you please look -- it may be on the second page. And let me give a copy to my assistant here so we can get some help. It's the paragraph starting at the bottom of page 2, "U sportskoj hali civili." Do you see that? On page 2, near the bottom there's a paragraph that starts "U sportskoj hali civili." Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Look down in that paragraph and you'll see a sentence that begins: "Organizatori i izvrsioci", "the organisers and perpetrators." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That sentence in the translation I have reads as follows. "The organisers and perpetrators of this expulsion of Bosniaks were SOS members, who had the blessing of the SDS Crisis Staff." Is that what you told Mr. Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I knew and what I told Mr. Ibric. If you have any further questions, I will be glad to elaborate on this subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the blessing of the SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The realisation that this would happen and not to try and prevent the tragedy of those people in Mahala, but they were let loose, as Rasula would put it. So I won't use the exact words out of respect. And the late Njunja, the head of the SOS, and Boro Tadic, the secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence who went from one house to the next in Mahala saying what should be burnt and what should not. He was a member of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today that meeting you had with Mr. Sergio De Mello, took place on 19 August 1992 and you were absolutely certain about that date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you actually pulled a book out of your pocket, a UN booklet of some kind, that you said was given to you by Mr. Sergio De Mello on that date, and you wrote the date in it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you can look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've had that book with you since that day that you went to meet with Mr. Sergio De Mello?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was among my documents that I carried to Travnik. I took my football literature with me, and this was amongst it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you will look, please, at the bottom of page 3 of your statement to Ibric, the last line. It has that date, [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that? It's the bottom of page 3. There's a "3" at the top -- right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. And if necessary, I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute. If you continue that sentence over to page 4, it says: "On 19 August 1992 we went to Dvor Na Uni together with Vrkes, a man called Eso, a military policeman. But we did not find the head of UNPROFOR there and had to go back. After a few days they established contact and enabled us to leave for Topusko for talks with Mr. Sergio De Mello. Now, according to your statement to Zihad Ibric, it was a few days after 19 August that you went to see Sergio De Mello. Now, what's correct, your testimony today or what you told Mr. Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said today is correct. And this is obviously an error. The first trip was to Dvor Na Uni, and then after that a meeting was scheduled with UNPROFOR and a certain Mr. Sergio. I know that it was the 19th of August, as it was -- as far as I know that today is Tuesday. So this was just a mix-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your mix-up or Mr. Ibric's mix-up?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine. Certainly. Allow me the possibility of mixing things up at the time in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do allow that. Please understand, I do. Go please to the next page. It's actually page 4. You're on that page, I guess. At the bottom of page 4 you see a paragraph -- it's the first paragraph up from the bottom. It says: "On 11 October 1992."

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second sentence of that you say this: "I know that the religious buildings were mostly destroyed by members of the SOS and Nedeljko Rasula was the one who gave the order for it." Tell me how you know that Rasula gave the order. Did you hear him give the order?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be glad to answer your question. I can claim with certainty that that is correct, that the mentioned members of the Serbian defence forces did it. I had occasion to see those guys in the building of the Sanski Most municipality. I had occasion to see their arrogant behaviour in the municipality when they broke into Mr. Rasula's office and took his pistol out. So it was common knowledge in Sanski Most that these guys belonged to the top of the SDS that Rasula belonged to, and they addressed him in the municipality as far as I was able to see. And I saw other delegations coming from Banja Luka to see Mr. Rasula. So I stand by what you just read out, that those guys were under the protection and instructions of the president at that time, that is, Mr. Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many -- how many religious buildings did you actually see them destroy?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with certainty the religious building where I live, it's about 150 or 200 metres away as the crows fly from my house. The central religious building in the Mahala Street in Sanski Most was also blown up. I saw this with my own eyes. There was a beautiful building in Caplje that could be seen from kilometres away. And as you looked from Pobrijezje towards Caplje the minaret was missing. I can claim with certainty about these three, but believe me I'm telling the truth when I say the 26 of them were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you actually saw members of SOS destroy these three that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, allow me. If I had seen it and if I was with them, I wouldn't be sitting here and I wouldn't be telling you this. I told you what the status of Muslims was. As soon as dusk fell, one had to rush home and lock up the doors. But there were stories in town, and it is common knowledge. My teacher Peda Mutic, a radical, took part in blowing up the mosque in Sanski Most. Unfortunately a Muslim woman breast-fed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't actually see -- now, the truth is you didn't actually see members of SOS destroy any religious buildings, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered that. He's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's an illusion, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's an illusion?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you know the truth, and you're asking me, a man who is not of your profession and putting me into an embarrassing situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to enter into an argument with counsel. Just answer his questions -- this is why I gave you this advice in the beginning. Just answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. The moment you move outside of those perimeters that I have explained to you, you are in trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But when I asked him -- when I said he has already answered that question, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information do you have that Nedeljko Rasula ordered members of SOS to destroy religious buildings? Specifically what information?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specific information is the knowledge in town, and this knowledge could not have come from Muslim sources. Allow for other possibilities of information. And there are witnesses - I can't name them - who saw Mutic, who saw the SOS, and logic tells me, knowing the attitudes, the relationships, the behaviour, the announcement of Mihajlo Orlovic on Radio Sana. He was a second Dzogo in Sanski Most. These men were praised and had no opinions of their own unfortunately we played football and handball together, but Medeni forgot who he had grown up with and what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it the answer to my question is you don't have any information of your own personal knowledge regarding an order given by Rasula. It's just a rumour that you heard around town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, am I allowed to give an indirect answer to this question in one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear what the indirect question is -- answer is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The spot on Radio Sana was such that our blood froze in our veins. Will we -- what are we waiting for? Surely the president of a municipality can have influence over the radio programmes. And if he can't stand the Muslim people, he could do this in a proper manner. Instead of allowing such a spot to be broadcast. Shall we. What are we waiting for?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to be shown a copy of the English version of your statement to the OTP, please. You've now been given the English version of your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. And I want to -- I want you to look at the bottom of the first page. You see a signature there. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first -- no. The cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn back one page. There. Right there. The bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to sign my name in front of you to see? Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just answer the question. The question is: Is that your signature? Just answer yes or no. I think you have answered yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look now, please, to your statement to Mr. Zijad Ibric. And each page has a signature. I'd like to ask you if that's your signature.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so sure. I have three ways of signing my name. That's true. Possibly in those days, in view of the condition that I was in, that this is my signature. The same text, Your Honour, was signed by me before I received this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to give you a blank piece of paper and a pen and ask you to make your signature three or four times on this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before you do so, Mr. Ackerman, and before he signs, could the usher show the witness his other statement of 13/2/1995, the statement released to Besim -- to Josip Ljubez. Do you have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I refer you to the bottom of each of these two pages, where it shows that there is a signature which should be your signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And here it is -- do you see or do you recognise that it is quite different from the other signature on the statement released to Zijad Ibric two days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. There's a visible difference. In this second one you see IB Islamcevic, and in the first one just Islamcevic Besim. But this is not one statement but two statements and two different dates. And I see it quite logical for me to be able to sign it in one way once and in another way the second way a different way. In Topusko I signed my name in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These statements are two days apart, sir, as His Honour has pointed out. Would it make that much difference in your signature just in two days?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a second means life at Grabez, not to mention two days in Travnik. A second could save your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you hand this to him and have him to sign it a few times for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to put your signature on here about four times, sir. Or if you want me to sign it more, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Different -- yes, exactly. Because Mr. Islamcevic you told us that you have three different kinds of signatures -- or I don't know how many you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a fourth in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So could you give us a specimen of each and every one of these different signatures and perhaps with each signature you repeat it once or -- repeat it twice or three times, because I recognise that each signature, even if it's always the same one, always comes out a little bit different each time you put it down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [the witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that signed in red or black?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know exactly where you are arriving --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have to give it back to him and have him sign again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keep this as well, please. But do give him another blank page. And please sign in black, in a dark -- not in red. I have a dark -- a black pen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've got the black pen. I gave it to him before. But I don't have another piece of paper. But I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I'm pretty sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The registry has saved us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We've got plenty of those. It's something that is never missing here, papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask the registrar to give us two exhibit numbers, have the one in red the first number, the one in black the second number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So the one in red will be DB89. The one in black will be DB90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the usher would be kind enough to make us photocopies straight away so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would like -- I would like to have the original for obvious purposes, Your Honour, and a copy be placed in the record at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you told us at one point in your testimony that up until a certain point in time relations between Muslims and Serbs in Sanski Most had been good.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the conflict broke out -- or rather, up until the multi-party elections and the formation of national parties, relations were good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was -- was that a genuinely good relationship between Muslims and Serbs, or was it enforced in some way?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, they were normal. They were as between human beings, as they should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were friendships there was respect, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some very nice examples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even mixed marriages; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 2 per cent in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting that you went to in Topusko, were you told -- did Vrkes or Rasula tell you or did you learn from my other way who it was from the RS -- Republika Srpska government that organised that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was organised by Mr. Vrkes Vlado. I don't know who he talked to for the meeting to take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that he talked to somebody at the higher level of the Republika Srpska government to get that accomplished?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to say, because I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's fine. I'm only asking what you know. During your testimony you've been writing things on a little piece of paper over there. What are you writing down?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't mind, please have a look -- or I shall bring the notes to you. Just notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really don't want to look at them. They're just notes of what's going on here today? Is that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I'll be glad to let you look at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure you weren't drawing caricatures of us lawyers or something.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If I were to make any drawings, it would be patterns for a football game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many Muslims remained in Sanski Most during the entire period of time that the Serbs were in charge there?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not quite specific, but I assume -- I can tell you up to the moment while I was there - that's, the 9th of February, 1995 - will you be satisfied with such an answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my own rough estimate, about 3.500 in February 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At one point in your testimony when you're talking about this meeting that you had had in Banja Luka where you spoke with Karadzic, you looked over this way and you said something like, "Perhaps Mr. Brdjanin knows this better than me." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't actually see Mr. Brdjanin in Banja Luka that day, did you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the point. I think he passed along the corridor and that I did see him, but I was not able - and I don't wish to claim that - but intimately I feel that he was present at that meeting, because knowing who came, knowing the hierarchy, it was not logical for him not to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's more of an assumption on your part that he would have been there than anything, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite frank in this courtroom and say that I cannot confirm that, but deep down I feel I saw him and that he was present, because I knew the gentleman from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about your brother. And I want to express my sympathy for what happened to your brother. Did your brother come from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other -- were there other people from Sanski Most that -- that wound up fighting in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank God. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer your first question now, with regard to my late brother, if you're interested. And I think you have more information for other cases than I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think maybe the question was misunderstood. My question was: Do you know how many men from Sanski Most fought in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you don't know, just tell me.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't you think you're asking me a bit too much? Aren't you asking me for too much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't know, just say I don't know. It's -- this is why I told you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact number. I really don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that other people from Sanski Most -- when I asked you about other people from Sanski Most that wound up fighting in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you said, "Yes, thank God." What did you mean by saying, "Thank God"?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant quite a lot by that. If not for such people, if they hadn't have given their lives, most probably I wouldn't be sitting here today in the courtroom, in this venerable -- before this venerable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Zecevic, I suppose you can start today, and then if you don't finish, we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I will not finish today since we have just ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Islamcevic, you're not going to be cross-examined by Mr. Zecevic, who is lead counsel for General Talic. Cross-examined by Mr. Zecevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Zecevic and I will put a few questions to you. Because of -- for the sake of the interpreters, when you answer my question, could you please make a pause because we understand each other but it is necessary for the interpreters to interpret what we say. Mr. Islamcevic, I want you to go back to your testimony before this Trial Chamber and I want to go back to the testimony that you gave yesterday. At the very beginning of the testimony that you gave, when my learned colleagues were examining you, you said that on the 25th of May, 1992 you were at the market as a foreman. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your colleague Vojo Milorad -- Vojin Save Milorad -- please wait for a minute, make a pause, and then answer the question. This colleague and friend of yours, Vojin Save Milorad, he warned you then that something was brewing in the town and that it was necessary for you to hand over the cash and that you should take shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 25th of May, 1992 you worked as a foreman for whom exactly? For a company? For an institution?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that question? Yes, I was working as a foreman at the market -- at the town market in Sanski Most as part of the communal services, the working unit of the communal services in Sanski Most. So as not to confuse you, in the future, at the beginning of April, I was moved from that station in Zdena from the water pump station to a new work -- working position. I don't want there to be confusion why was I first in Zdena and then at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just proceed slowly and we shall clarify everything then. In the statement that you gave to investigators for the Prosecution in 1999 you said that you worked in the communal services in the funeral parlour department. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That department was called the working department for communal services. And the work description of the foreman -- the chief of the funeral services was Dragutin Petar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words it is the same work post.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two -- two different sets of duties are involved, but it is one single post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, a minute ago you tried to clarify this for us. Before that you worked at the pump station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that pump station did you also take that post just before the spring of 1992? Did you take up that post on that date or earlier on?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that post by virtue of the decision of Lukic Mladen, director of the company. Up until then I was involved in work protection and I went to Novi Sad to obtain a certificate in a committee there. That's where I got the certificate. I wasn't to the -- I didn't suit the gentleman in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may ask the usher -- because I am following the translation just not to -- to speed it up too much. But I cannot hear what the witness is answering because the -- the microphones are a bit too apart. So I don't hear the original, actually, which I am listening with my ears. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem, I'll -- I'll approach the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as you said it was the director's decision - who didn't like you - you were transferred to the pump station. That was the director's decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Afterwards, in April, you were transferred to this other working position at the market.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six months before April I was assigned duties at the pump station in Zdena. I was in charge. And through agreements reached between the parties, the director's post belonged to the SDA -- Ahmet Paunovic came as director. And I was a member of the SDP, as I am today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, please concentrate on the question and just answer the question, because there's too much information which really isn't relevant to us. I understand that you want to explain things.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer all your questions, sir. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you: Is it correct to say that in April 1992 you were transferred from that post, the pump station in Zdena, to the market?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And to the shop where funeral equipment, funeral items were sold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were the foreman there.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time this same person, Mladen Lukic, was the director of the communal services.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ahmet Paunovic came as director. He was an engineer, a geodetics engineer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he decided to transfer you to that market; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be -- because I am moving to another matter. Would it be okay if I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Islamcevic. I'll see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of how long you anticipate your cross-examination to last, so that Mr. Cayley or whoever will be taking up the next witness can plan ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honours it depends entirely on the answers by this witness. Because I anticipated one hour to one hour and a half. But it might be longer because I will have to hear the answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a slight problem tomorrow because the witness who is next, as you know, is very unwell. He doesn't arrive in The Hague until this evening. So we need to make an assessment tomorrow whether he will be ready to testify tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have only got one coming. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct. So we will be able to give you an answer at the beginning of tomorrow's session or maybe somewhat before that through the registry as to whether or not he will be ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're talking of 7.119 or 7.59?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We're moving straight to 7.59, because 7.119 is the individual who will essentially lose his job if he comes to testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So that is the position we are in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. But in any case, tomorrow we'll proceed with the cross-examination -- last cross-examination of this witness. And then we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll see where we are. I mean, I'll let you know, Your Honours, as soon as I can where we are with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The indication is that he's still arriving in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So maybe we are worrying for nothing. Let's hope so. Mr. Ackerman, before we adjourn, earlier on you raised something with regard to the transportation which I promised to look into. I wanted to know if this is something that has surfaced now or whether it's something that has been happening since we've been having sittings in the afternoon and finishing at 6.30 instead of 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it partly relates to the fact that we are finishing ahead of -- of other Chambers, and they're probably trying to do their transportation all at the same time. I'm not certain of that. But certainly I understand last night it was not until 7.30 -- and I'm being told that's not the problem. So I think it's been going on quite a long time. And I really don't know very much about it other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think I would rather have full information before you speak out. I mean, if Mr. Brdjanin or whatever wants -- yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm perfectly comfortable with Mr. Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to go in private session, we can go in private session. But it's -- Yes, Mr. Brdjanin. Tell me what's happening, that's all. And very briefly. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] As far as the entire stay here is concerned, I have nothing to object to. But we don't understand why we have to wait for an hour when we are alone, and that is not a recent thing. This happens every day. And if I say almost every day, then maybe it doesn't happen on a day or two. Last time there was no one there apart from us. We were 45 minutes -- we were there for 45 minutes and then they said, "You're going down to the room downstairs?" I said, "Why? We won't have time to have dinner. We won't do anything." I'll tell you what the reason is. I don't think that anyone wants a -- a break. We are elderly people. We'll just get ill if we wait for over an hour every day, if we have to wait for over an hour every day. And there is no reason for this, I think, because there are two cars -- they have two cars. But I don't know how this is organised. I can't enter into these matters. This happens very frequently, very frequently. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. When it happens, does it affect your dinner at the Detention Centre? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] How should I put it? We arrive -- we barely arrive in time. We don't have time to do anything then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Microphone not activated] I think Mr. Islamcevic, you will be escorted -- you will be escorted out of the courtroom now and taken to your hotel and then we'll see you again tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. Hopefully we won't keep you waiting half an hour like we did today. Hopefully we should be in a position to start at 2.15 sharp. The usher will take care of you. Thank you. We are adjourned till tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.
